0027 — Keep fixtures out of scanners' sight with neutral names, not dismissals

Status: accepted

Problem

Offing's tests need repositories that deliberately contain old lockfiles, manifests, and Dockerfiles. Those files are what the detectors read, so they must stay realistic. Dependency scanners read them too and report them as the project's own risk. Epic #1981 needs one written way to stop that before any later task moves a file.

On 2026-11-04, main commits 1,521 files under tests/fixtures/, and 179 of them carry a name that package tooling recognizes (57 Dockerfile, 24 package-lock.json, 17 composer.lock, 13 pubspec.lock, 13 go.mod, 12 pom.xml, 10 Gemfile.lock, and a tail of other lockfiles). The gap is real; this record picks the method only.

Options compared

Option What it is Where it lives
Neutral names Commit Gemfile.lock as Gemfile.lock.fixture; tests copy the tree into a temporary directory and restore the real name there. Repository files plus a test helper.
Real names in a temporary directory Tests write the whole fixture from a description at run time; nothing manifest-shaped is committed. Test code.
Archives Commit fixtures.tar.gz or .zip and unpack it in a test. One binary per group.
Scanner configuration Keep real names and tell each scanner to skip them (osv-scanner.toml, ignore lists). Config files.
Dismissal Close each alert as "used in tests" in the scanner's UI. Outside the repository.

Measurements

Tools: OSV-Scanner v2 (scan source -r) and OpenSSF Scorecard v5 (--local), both built from their latest release on 2026-11-04; Node.js v26.12.0; network on for the advisory lookup only. Variants used the fixtures ruby/positive/Gemfile.lock, php/positive/composer.lock, rust/positive/Cargo.lock, java/positive/spring-boot/pom.xml, and upgrade/poetry-lock/ready/poetry.lock, copied into scratch directories under each storage method.

Today

Check Result on main
OSV-Scanner over the checkout 24 sources with known vulnerabilities; 16 are under tests/fixtures/, the rest are examples/, the root lockfile, and extensions/vscode.
Scorecard Vulnerabilities Score 0, 85 existing vulnerabilities.
Scorecard Pinned-Dependencies Score 3; 133 of 136 warnings are in tests/fixtures/ or examples/.

Storage methods against OSV-Scanner

The same five files, scanned per variant:

Variant Vulnerabilities reported
Real names (control) 50, across all five files
<name>.txt 0 (no packages found)
<name>.fixture 0 (no packages found)
fixture-<name> 0 (no packages found)
.tar.gz and .zip of the real tree 0 (no packages found)
Real names, directory in .gitignore 0, but --no-ignore brings back 50; and ignored files are not committed
Real names, osv-scanner.toml PackageOverrides with ignore = true 0

OSV-Scanner matches lockfiles by exact file name, so any rename hides them.

Storage methods against Scorecard

Variant Vulnerabilities Pinned-Dependencies
Real names (control) score 0, 44 vulnerabilities Dockerfile found, 3 warnings
Lockfiles renamed to <name>.txt score 10, none not applicable
Lockfiles with real names plus osv-scanner.toml score 10, none (Scorecard reads the file) not applicable
Dockerfile.txt, Dockerfile.fixture, fixture.dockerfile, dockerfile.in not applicable still found
image.fixture, base.txt, fixture.df, Containerfile not applicable not found

Scorecard recognizes a Dockerfile by the case-insensitive word dockerfile anywhere in the name, so a suffix is not enough for that family. Scorecard's Pinned-Dependencies check has no configuration that skips a file.

Not measured

GitHub's dependency graph and Dependabot alerts were not run; the pull request that adds this record cannot trigger them on new files. GitHub documents the graph as reading supported manifests by file name, which matches what OSV-Scanner and Scorecard did above. The implementation task must confirm this on a real pull request, using the Security tab.

Decision

  1. Commit fixtures under neutral names. Any fixture file whose real name a scanner recognizes is stored with a .fixture suffix (Gemfile.lock.fixture). Tests build the scanned repository in a temporary directory, copy each tree there, and drop the suffix. The detectors still read real names, so detector behavior is unchanged and the committed tree holds nothing scanner-shaped.
  2. The Dockerfile family gets a different rule. Names that contain dockerfile stay visible to Scorecard with a suffix, so the stored name must not contain that word; the helper maps it back. The exact stored spelling is chosen by the implementation task and verified with the guard in point 4.
  3. Fixtures that the tests build from a description stay allowed. A test that already writes its files into a temporary directory needs nothing committed and keeps doing so. Use it when a fixture is only a few lines.
  4. Guard the rule in npm run check. A test fails when a committed path under tests/fixtures/ has a name from the recognized-manifest list, so a new fixture cannot reintroduce the problem. The same list drives the helper.
  5. Reject archives. They hide the content from review and diffs and change as a whole for a one-line edit. They add nothing the rename does not: both hid the files equally in the measurements.
  6. Reject dismissal as the main method. A dismissal is a per-alert decision made outside the repository, is not reviewed in a pull request, must be repeated for each new fixture and each new advisory, and does nothing for the Scorecard score, which counts vulnerabilities from OSV whatever the repository's alert state.
  7. Scanner configuration is a narrow fallback, not the method. osv-scanner.toml works for OSV-Scanner and Scorecard Vulnerabilities (measured above), but it suppresses by ecosystem and directory, grows with every fixture, cannot reach Pinned-Dependencies or GitHub alerts, and is a suppression list in all but name. Use it only for a file whose real name a test cannot avoid, with a written reason next to the entry.

Why

  • The only method that works for every scanner. Renaming removes the file from OSV-Scanner, Scorecard Vulnerabilities, and (by their documented file-name matching) GitHub's graph. Configuration reaches two of the four surfaces measured or documented.
  • Honest about the exception. Dockerfiles are matched by a substring, and the measurements show a plain suffix fails there, so the decision names the exception instead of promising one rule.
  • Reviewable and local. The files are in the repository, diff as text, and are checked by a test. Nothing depends on a UI action that a contributor could skip.

Consequences

  • A follow-up task adds the copy helper, renames the 179 recognized files, updates the tests that point at tests/fixtures/ directly, and adds the guard from point 4. This record changes no file under tests/.
  • examples/ holds 8 of the 24 OSV sources today. It is outside this decision; whether it takes the same rule or another is a separate question for the epic.
  • The project's own manifests (root package-lock.json and extensions/vscode/package-lock.json) stay visible and keep being fixed by upgrades, not hidden.
  • No runtime dependency and no network use in scans. The scanners were run only to produce the evidence above.
